title: The first words after
hook: he returns and says there is no Hindu and no Muslim, and the town asks what he means

segments.voice: Yesterday: three days in the river, and a man who walked out of the Bein. Your line was some come back changed. Who did you go easy on? Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THREE DAYS IN THE RIVER — SOME COME BACK CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The whole town has mourned him. They dragged the river. His sister wept. And then, on the third morning, he walks back into Sultanpur, alive, soaking wet, with a look on his face nobody can read. People crowd around. Where were you? What happened? Are you all right? And the stories say he didn't answer. For a while he said nothing at all. He gave away what he owned and sat in silence. The town waited for an explanation. When he finally spoke, it wasn't an explanation. It was one short sentence, and it set the whole town talking. Today, the first words after.
screen: `THE TOWN HAD MOURNED HIM.` → `HE WALKS BACK IN, SILENT.` → `ONE SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence, as tradition remembers it: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. You met it back on day six, as that day's line. Now you know where it comes from. Look at where he said it. Sultanpur was a town ruled by a Muslim governor, full of Hindu merchants and Muslim officials, temples and mosques, each community with its own rules about food, prayer and who you could marry. Who you were showed in your food, your prayers, your clothes. And the storekeeper who'd just come back from the dead says: neither. What did he mean? The sources don't include a footnote, so Sikhs and scholars have heard it in several ways, and it's worth hearing each. Some Sikhs hear it this way: before God, there are no labels. Beneath the Hindu and the Muslim, there are just people, all made by the one, Ik Onkar. Others hear a challenge: nobody around him was truly living up to what their faith asked. The real Hindu, the real Muslim, was hard to find, and he was calling both back to the heart of their own paths. And some hear a third thing too: the first sign of a new path, one that wouldn't be defined by either community. These readings don't cancel each other out, and they can be held together. What the sentence clearly isn't is contempt. Nanak spent the rest of his life sitting with Hindus and Muslims, praying, singing, eating, arguing gently, and his companion on the road, Mardana, was a Muslim. Of course the town asked what he meant. And the town's religious judge, the qazi, decided to find out for himself. That's tomorrow.
screen: `THERE IS NO HINDU, THERE IS NO MUSLIM.` · `A TOWN WHERE LABELS WERE EVERYTHING.` · `NO LABELS, A CHALLENGE, A NEW PATH.` · `NOT CONTEMPT.` · then, large: `BENEATH THE LABELS, PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and think about the labels you put on people without meaning to: liberal, conservative, rich, poor, old, young, religious, not. Pick one you use often. Now bring to mind one real person you'd put that label on. Slowly peel it off. Who's underneath? Someone who gets tired, who loves someone, who's afraid of something. Stay with that person, without the label, for a while. The bell holds the time.
The first words after. Back from the river, Nanak says: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.
Your line: beneath the labels, people. Today, notice one label you put on someone, and set it aside for one conversation. Day twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's words after the river as the start of his mission, and often quote them as a teaching that all people are one before God.

fork.setup: you've come back after three days. the whole town is asking what happened. what do you say first?
options: tell them every detail of what you saw.
stay silent, then say: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.
go straight back to work at the storehouse.
fork.reveal: the stories say he was silent, gave away what he owned, and then spoke one sentence that set the town talking.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: no one is Hindu, no one Muslim, the words tradition gives him.

trapdoor: what you thought: Nanak rejected both religions.
what it means: beneath the labels, people, all made by the one. and a call to live the heart of whatever path you're on.
what a scholar hears: the saying comes from the janamsakhis, not from a hymn. its setting in Sultanpur, under a Muslim governor with a mixed population, gives it its edge.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi traditions (Guru Nanak's words after the Bein: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim)
Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1 (the Sultanpur narrative)

notes: The saying is paraphrased/translated in the voice without a named translation (quoted: null). Macauliffe renders it (from memory) as 'There is no Hindu and no Musalman'; verify before quoting.
Gurmukhi of the saying (ਨਾ ਕੋ ਹਿੰਦੂ ਨਾ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਨ) follows the common form 'na ko Hindu na Musalman'; confirm spelling.
Three readings are given without ranking; Keepers should confirm each is fairly described, especially 'the first sign of a new path', which some Sikhs stress and others downplay.
The period of silence and giving away possessions follows common tellings; confirm.
